newsitem.title: ZAIRE: U.N. repatriates refugees from Zaire.
newsitem.headline: U.N. repatriates refugees from Zaire.

text.p: The U.N. refugee agency started repatriating 3,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees from Zaire on Wednesday and a U.N. investigator accused rebels of massacring the Hutus late last year.
The rebels meanwhile dismissed the nomination of Etienne Tshisekedi by the opposition in Kinshasa as Zaire's new prime minister on Tuesday as making no difference to their goal.

Peter Kessler, a spokesman for the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) in Goma city, said the agency expected to have repatriated 3,000 Hutu refugees by truck to Rwanda from Karuba by the end of Wednesday.
Aid officials said 20,000 refugees remained at Karuba west of Goma and they expected sites at Tingi Tingi and Amisi were emptied of refugees by two flights on Wednesday to Goma for repatriation.

Kessler said the highest death rate appeared to be at km 82 (mile 50) south of the rebel-held northeastern capital of Kisangani where about half the 800 refugees there in mid-March had died of malnutrition, malaria, sickness and their wounds.
He said aid agency staff clearing shelters at Lula, seven km (four miles) south of Kisangani, found 50 bodies on Monday of refugees who had died from exhaustion, sickness or malnutrition.

The rebels ordered 20,000 refugees to leave Lula on Monday and join another 60,000 farther south of Kisangani for security reasons. The rebels fear they include former Rwandan Hutu troops and militiamen who fought alongside Zairean government troops.
In Geneva, a U.N. human rights investigator accused the rebels of massacring Rwandan refugees during their push across the region late last year and urged a speedy investigation.
Roberto Garreton said upon his return from a three-day visit to Goma that the rebels had failed to come up with satisfactory answers to allegations of killings, torture and disappearances.

At a news conference, Garreton said eyewitness accounts of the number of people killed by the rebels ranged from hundreds to 50,000 and demanded a detailed probe by independent experts to be appointed by the U.N. Human Rights Commission in Geneva.
"There were massacres by the rebels. That's for sure. There's an enormous list of allegations of massacres but it is impossible to give numbers," the Chilean investigator said.
Zaire accuses Rwanda's Tutsi-dominated army and Ugandan troops of supporting the rebels, but they deny these charges.

"I can't say that the Rwandan and Ugandan armies are there with their generals and colonels. But the local people view the rebel forces as an occupation army. It is clear that these rebels are not Zaireans," Garreton said.
The rebel force led by Laurent Kabila is dominated by ethnic Tutsis, some said by intelligence sources to be Rwandan troops.
Demobilised Ugandan troops, hired on contract, are also part of the rebel force. Kabila is a Zairean non-Tutsi from Shaba and his field commanders are a mixture of Zaireans and foreigners.
The opposition in Kinshasa nominated Tshisekedi, President Mobutu Sese Seko's arch-foe, on Tuesday as Zaire's new prime minister to steer Zaire through negotiations with the rebels.
"It won't make any difference. Our purpose is to get rid of Mobutu and we will push until we have got him out," said Mwenze Kongolo, rebel alliance justice commissioner, on Wednesday.
Kongolo said that Tshisekedi, 64, was probably best-known in the capital Kinshasa and his appointment might have some weight there "but the rest of the country is waiting for us".
Many Zairean politicians said they expected the ailing Mobutu to move quickly to sign Tshisekedi's appointment into law to succeed prime minister Kengo wa Dondo, who resigned a week ago.
Tshisekedi has huge popular backing in Zaire but support for Kabila has grown as rebels seized a quarter of the country.
